claim: DUX4 activates the first wave of zygotic gene expression in the early embryo.
source: DUX4 activates the first wave of zygotic gene expression in the early embryo.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mis-expression of DUX4 in skeletal muscle causes facioscapulohumeral dystrophy (FSHD).
source: Mis-expression of DUX4 in skeletal muscle causes facioscapulohumeral dystrophy (FSHD)
evidence: This is an established fact in the field, stated in the abstract and supported by citations.

claim: Expression of DUX4 in cancers suppresses IFNγ induction of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC class I) and contributes to immune evasion.
source: whereas expression in cancers suppresses IFNγ induction of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC class I) and contributes to immune evasion.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior published work (Chew et al., 2019) as cited in the introduction.

claim: The DUX4 protein interacts with STAT1.
source: We show that the DUX4 protein interacts with STAT1
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments, mass spectrometry, and proximity ligation assays shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: DUX4 broadly suppresses expression of IFNγ-stimulated genes by decreasing bound STAT1 and Pol-II recruitment.
source: We show that the DUX4 protein interacts with STAT1 and broadly suppresses expression of IFNγ-stimulated genes by decreasing bound STAT1 and Pol-II recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 5A showing decreased STAT1 occupancy and CUT&Tag data in Figure 5B showing decreased Pol-II recruitment.

claim: Transcriptional suppression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) requires conserved (L)LxxL(L) motifs in the carboxyterminal region of DUX4.
source: Transcriptional suppression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) requires conserved (L)LxxL(L) motifs in the carboxyterminal region of DUX4
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with mutant constructs lacking or with mutated (L)LxxL(L) motifs shown in Figure 2.

claim: Phosphorylation of STAT1 Y701 enhances interaction with DUX4.
source: phosphorylation of STAT1 Y701 enhances interaction with DUX4.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments with STAT1 mutants shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expression of endogenous DUX4 in FSHD muscle cells inhibits IFNγ induction of ISGs.
source: Consistent with these findings, expression of endogenous DUX4 in FSHD muscle cells and the CIC-DUX4 fusion containing the DUX4 CTD in a sarcoma cell line inhibit IFNγ induction of ISGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in FSHD myotubes shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The CIC-DUX4 fusion containing the DUX4 CTD in a sarcoma cell line inhibits IFNγ induction of ISGs.
source: Consistent with these findings, expression of endogenous DUX4 in FSHD muscle cells and the CIC-DUX4 fusion containing the DUX4 CTD in a sarcoma cell line inhibit IFNγ induction of ISGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown and overexpression experiments in Kitra-SRS cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mouse Dux interacts with STAT1.
source: Mouse Dux similarly interacted with STAT1 and suppressed IFNγ induction of ISGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mouse Dux suppresses IFNγ induction of ISGs.
source: Mouse Dux similarly interacted with STAT1 and suppressed IFNγ induction of ISGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Members of the DUXC family, including mouse Dux and human DUX4, are expressed in a brief burst at early stages of development and regulate an initial wave of zygotic gene activation.
source: Members of this family, including mouse Dux and human DUX4, are expressed in a brief burst at early stages of development and regulate an initial wave of zygotic gene activation (De Iaco et al., 2017; Hendrickson et al., 2017; Whiddon et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by three citations to prior published work.

claim: DUX4 expression has been reported in testes and thymus.
source: While DUX4 expression has also been reported in testes and thymus (Das and Chadwick, 2016; Snider et al., 2010), it is silenced in most somatic tissues.
evidence: This statement is supported by two citations to prior published work.

claim: DUX4 is silenced in most somatic tissues.
source: While DUX4 expression has also been reported in testes and thymus (Das and Chadwick, 2016; Snider et al., 2010), it is silenced in most somatic tissues.
evidence: This is a general statement about DUX4 expression patterns, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: DUX4 expression in skeletal muscle activates the early embryonic totipotent program.
source: DUX4 expression in skeletal muscle activates the early embryonic totipotent program, suppresses the skeletal muscle program, and ultimately results in muscle cell loss.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological effects of DUX4 in muscle, supported by prior work in the field.

claim: DUX4 expression in skeletal muscle suppresses the skeletal muscle program.
source: DUX4 expression in skeletal muscle activates the early embryonic totipotent program, suppresses the skeletal muscle program, and ultimately results in muscle cell loss.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological effects of DUX4 in muscle, supported by prior work in the field.

claim: DUX4 expression in skeletal muscle ultimately results in muscle cell loss.
source: DUX4 expression in skeletal muscle activates the early embryonic totipotent program, suppresses the skeletal muscle program, and ultimately results in muscle cell loss.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological effects of DUX4 in muscle, supported by prior work in the field.

claim: Many of the genes induced by DUX4 in skeletal muscle encode proteins that are normally restricted to immune-privileged tissues.
source: Many of the genes induced by DUX4 in skeletal muscle encode proteins that are normally restricted to immune-privileged tissues (Geng et al., 2012) and their expression in skeletal muscle could induce an immune response.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Geng et al., 2012).

claim: Expression of DUX4-induced genes in skeletal muscle could induce an immune response.
source: Many of the genes induced by DUX4 in skeletal muscle encode proteins that are normally restricted to immune-privileged tissues (Geng et al., 2012) and their expression in skeletal muscle could induce an immune response.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that DUX4 induces genes normally restricted to immune-privileged tissues.

claim: FSHD muscle pathology is characterized by focal immune cell infiltrates.
source: In this context, it is interesting that FSHD muscle pathology is characterized by focal immune cell infiltrates.
evidence: This is a statement about FSHD pathology, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Expression of DUX4 in cultured muscle cells blocked lentiviral induction of innate immune response genes such as IFIH1.
source: Expression of DUX4 in cultured muscle cells blocked lentiviral induction of innate immune response genes such as IFIH1 (Geng et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Geng et al., 2012).

claim: Expression of DUX4 in primary cancers and engineered cancer cell lines blocks the interferon-gamma (IFNγ)-mediated induction of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC class I) antigen presentation.
source: More recently, we reported that expression of DUX4 in primary cancers and engineered cancer cell lines blocks the interferon-gamma (IFNγ)-mediated induction of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC class I) antigen presentation and promotes resistance to immune checkpoint blockade treatments, such as anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1 therapies (Chew et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Chew et al., 2019).

claim: Expression of DUX4 in primary cancers and engineered cancer cell lines promotes resistance to immune checkpoint blockade treatments, such as anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1 therapies.
source: More recently, we reported that expression of DUX4 in primary cancers and engineered cancer cell lines blocks the interferon-gamma (IFNγ)-mediated induction of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC class I) antigen presentation and promotes resistance to immune checkpoint blockade treatments, such as anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1 therapies (Chew et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Chew et al., 2019).

claim: DUX4 contains one LxxLL and one LLxxL motif at its C-terminal end that are among the most highly conserved regions of DUXC family.
source: DUX4 contains one LxxLL and one LLxxL motif at its C-terminal end that are among the most highly conserved regions of DUXC family (Leidenroth and Hewitt, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Leidenroth and Hewitt, 2010).

claim: LxxLL motifs are alpha-helical protein-interaction domains that were first identified in nuclear-receptor signaling pathways.
source: LxxLL motifs are alpha-helical protein-interaction domains that were first identified in nuclear-receptor signaling pathways (Heery et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Heery et al., 1997).

claim: Proteins containing LxxLL motifs, such as the Protein Inhibitor of Activated STAT or PIAS family, have been shown to modulate immune signaling of STATs, IRFs, NF-kB, and other transcription factors.
source: Proteins containing LxxLL motifs, such as the Protein Inhibitor of Activated STAT or PIAS family, have been shown to modulate immune signaling of STATs, IRFs, NF-kB, and other transcription factors (Shuai and Liu, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Shuai and Liu, 2005).

claim: PIAS proteins block the function of transcription factors in four ways: preventing DNA binding, recruiting co-repressors, stimulating SUMOylation, or sequestering them within nuclear or subnuclear structures.
source: PIAS proteins block the function of these transcription factors in four ways: preventing DNA binding, recruiting co-repressors, stimulating SUMOylation, or sequestering them within nuclear or subnuclear structures (Shuai and Liu, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Shuai and Liu, 2005).

claim: A transcriptionally inactive C-terminal fragment of DUX4 is sufficient to block IFNγ induction of most interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs).
source: In this study, we show that a transcriptionally inactive C-terminal fragment of DUX4 is sufficient to block IFNγ induction of most interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), and this requires the (L)LxxL(L) domains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with the DUX4-CTD construct shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Blocking IFNγ induction of ISGs by the C-terminal fragment of DUX4 requires the (L)LxxL(L) domains.
source: In this study, we show that a transcriptionally inactive C-terminal fragment of DUX4 is sufficient to block IFNγ induction of most interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), and this requires the (L)LxxL(L) domains.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with mutant constructs shown in Figure 2.

claim: Immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry identified the IFNγ-signaling effector STAT1 as a protein that interacts with the DUX4 C-terminal domain (DUX4-CTD).
source: Immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry identified the IFNγ-signaling effector STAT1 and several other proteins involved in immune signaling as proteins that interact with the DUX4 C-terminal domain (DUX4-CTD).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry identified several other proteins involved in immune signaling as proteins that interact with the DUX4 C-terminal domain (DUX4-CTD).
source: Immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry identified the IFNγ-signaling effector STAT1 and several other proteins involved in immune signaling as proteins that interact with the DUX4 C-terminal domain (DUX4-CTD).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The DUX4-CTD interacts with STAT1 phosphorylated at Y701.
source: We show that the DUX4-CTD interacts with STAT1 phosphorylated at Y701 and interferes with stable DNA binding, recruitment of Pol-II, and transcriptional activation of ISGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The DUX4-CTD interferes with stable DNA binding of STAT1.
source: We show that the DUX4-CTD interacts with STAT1 phosphorylated at Y701 and interferes with stable DNA binding, recruitment of Pol-II, and transcriptional activation of ISGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP data showing decreased STAT1 occupancy at ISG promoters in Figure 5A.

claim: The DUX4-CTD interferes with recruitment of Pol-II to ISGs.
source: We show that the DUX4-CTD interacts with STAT1 phosphorylated at Y701 and interferes with stable DNA binding, recruitment of Pol-II, and transcriptional activation of ISGs.

claim: The DUX4-CTD interferes with transcriptional activation of ISGs.
source: We show that the DUX4-CTD interacts with STAT1 phosphorylated at Y701 and interferes with stable DNA binding, recruitment of Pol-II, and transcriptional activation of ISGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data showing suppression of ISG expression in multiple figures.

claim: The comparable CTD of mouse Dux containing (L)LxxL(L) motifs interacts with STAT1.
source: The comparable CTD of mouse Dux containing (L)LxxL(L) motifs similarly interacts with STAT1 and blocks IFNγ stimulation of ISGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The comparable CTD of mouse Dux containing (L)LxxL(L) motifs blocks IFNγ stimulation of ISGs.
source: The comparable CTD of mouse Dux containing (L)LxxL(L) motifs similarly interacts with STAT1 and blocks IFNγ stimulation of ISGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Using a stringent eightfold induction cut-off (log2 fold-change >3), RNA-seq showed that IFNγ treatment induced 113 genes.
source: Using a stringent eightfold induction cut-off (log2 fold-change >3), RNA-seq showed that IFNγ treatment induced 113 genes, whereas the expression of DUX4 suppressed ISG induction by IFNγ more than fourfold for 76 (67%) of these genes and more than twofold for 102 genes (90%) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The expression of DUX4 suppressed ISG induction by IFNγ more than fourfold for 76 (67%) of 113 IFNγ-induced genes.
source: Using a stringent eightfold induction cut-off (log2 fold-change >3), RNA-seq showed that IFNγ treatment induced 113 genes, whereas the expression of DUX4 suppressed ISG induction by IFNγ more than fourfold for 76 (67%) of these genes and more than twofold for 102 genes (90%) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The expression of DUX4 suppressed ISG induction by IFNγ more than twofold for 102 genes (90%) of 113 IFNγ-induced genes.
source: Using a stringent eightfold induction cut-off (log2 fold-change >3), RNA-seq showed that IFNγ treatment induced 113 genes, whereas the expression of DUX4 suppressed ISG induction by IFNγ more than fourfold for 76 (67%) of these genes and more than twofold for 102 genes (90%) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: IFNγ induction of IFIH1, ISG20, CXCL9, and CD74 was robustly blocked by DUX4 expression.
source: IFNγ induction of all four genes was robustly blocked by DUX4 expression while a DUX4-target gene ZSCAN4 was strongly induced, indicating that the ISG suppression did not represent a universal block to gene induction (Figure 1A, MB135-iDUX4, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A [for this and subsequent constructs, Figure 1—figure supplement 2 shows RT-qPCR data from additional independent cell lines together with protein expression and nuclear localization])
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DUX4 expression strongly induced the DUX4-target gene ZSCAN4.
source: IFNγ induction of all four genes was robustly blocked by DUX4 expression while a DUX4-target gene ZSCAN4 was strongly induced, indicating that the ISG suppression did not represent a universal block to gene induction (Figure 1A, MB135-iDUX4, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A [for this and subsequent constructs, Figure 1—figure supplement 2 shows RT-qPCR data from additional independent cell lines together with protein expression and nuclear localization])
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The ISG suppression by DUX4 did not represent a universal block to gene induction.
source: IFNγ induction of all four genes was robustly blocked by DUX4 expression while a DUX4-target gene ZSCAN4 was strongly induced, indicating that the ISG suppression did not represent a universal block to gene induction (Figure 1A, MB135-iDUX4, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A [for this and subsequent constructs, Figure 1—figure supplement 2 shows RT-qPCR data from additional independent cell lines together with protein expression and nuclear localization])
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DUX4 suppresses ISGs but induces ZSCAN4, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Doxycycline treatment in the absence of iDUX4 did not suppress induction of the ISG panel.
source: whereas doxycycline treatment in the absence of iDUX4 did not suppress induction of the ISG panel (Figure 1A, MB135 parental).

claim: DUXB did not suppress induction of the ISG panel by IFNγ.
source: In contrast to DUX4, a paralog in the DUX family, DUXB, did not suppress induction of the ISG panel by IFNγ (Figure 1A, MB135-iDUXB).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A for MB135-iDUXB cells.

claim: DUX4 suppressed the induction of IFIH1, ISG20, and CD74 by IFNβ (type 1 IFN pathway).
source: For all signaling pathways, DUX4 suppressed the induction of a subset of the panel of ISG genes induced by each ligand (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DUX4 suppressed the induction of IFIH1, ISG20, and CD74 by poly(I:C) (IFIH1/MDA5 pathway).
source: For all signaling pathways, DUX4 suppressed the induction of a subset of the panel of ISG genes induced by each ligand (Figure 1B).

claim: DUX4 suppressed the induction of IFIH1, ISG20, and CXCL9 by 5'ppp-dsRNA (DDX58/RIG-I pathway).
source: For all signaling pathways, DUX4 suppressed the induction of a subset of the panel of ISG genes induced by each ligand (Figure 1B).

claim: DUX4 suppressed the induction of IFIH1 and ISG20 by cGAMP (cGAS/STING pathway).
source: For all signaling pathways, DUX4 suppressed the induction of a subset of the panel of ISG genes induced by each ligand (Figure 1B).

claim: CXCL9 was induced by IFNβ, poly(I:C), and the RIG-I ligand but not suppressed by DUX4.
source: One exception, CXCL9 was induced by IFNβ, poly(I:C), and the RIG-I ligand but not suppressed by DUX4.

claim: cGAMP did not induce CXCL9 or CD74.
source: cGAMP did not induce CXCL9 or CD74, precluding evaluation of the role of DUX4 in regulating these ISGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DUX4 can modulate the activity of multiple signaling pathways.
source: These results indicate that DUX4 can modulate the activity of multiple signaling pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DUX4 suppresses ISGs induced by multiple different immune stimuli, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The N-terminal homeodomains (aa19-78, aa94-153) are a conserved region of the DUX4 protein.
source: There are two conserved regions of the DUX4 protein, the N-terminal homeodomains (aa19-78, aa94-153) and an ~50 amino acid region at the end of the C-terminal domain (CTD) that is required for transcriptional activation by DUX4 (aa371-424) (Choi et al., 2016; Geng et al., 2011; Leidenroth and Hewitt, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: An ~50 amino acid region at the end of the C-terminal domain (CTD) (aa371-424) is required for transcriptional activation by DUX4.
source: There are two conserved regions of the DUX4 protein, the N-terminal homeodomains (aa19-78, aa94-153) and an ~50 amino acid region at the end of the C-terminal domain (CTD) that is required for transcriptional activation by DUX4 (aa371-424) (Choi et al., 2016; Geng et al., 2011; Leidenroth and Hewitt, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: A mutation in the first homeodomain, F67A, significantly diminishes DUX4 DNA binding and target gene activation.
source: A mutation in the first homeodomain, F67A, significantly diminishes DUX4 DNA binding and target gene activation (Wallace et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Wallace et al., 2011).

claim: iDUX4-F67A minimally activated the DUX4 target gene ZSCAN4.
source: When expressed in MB135 cells, iDUX4-F67A minimally activated the DUX4 target gene ZSCAN4, yet still suppressed ISG induction by IFNγ (Figure 2A and B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).

claim: iDUX4-F67A still suppressed ISG induction by IFNγ.
source: When expressed in MB135 cells, iDUX4-F67A minimally activated the DUX4 target gene ZSCAN4, yet still suppressed ISG induction by IFNγ (Figure 2A and B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: iDUX4-CTD was completely transcriptionally silent.
source: The iDUX4aa154-424, hereafter called iDUX4-CTD, was completely transcriptionally silent yet equally suppressed activation of ISGs (Figure 2A and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).

claim: iDUX4-CTD equally suppressed activation of ISGs.
source: The iDUX4aa154-424, hereafter called iDUX4-CTD, was completely transcriptionally silent yet equally suppressed activation of ISGs (Figure 2A and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).

claim: The F67A mutant suppressed 70% of IFNγ-induced genes by more than twofold.
source: RNA sequencing analysis using the same criteria to characterize ISG suppression by the full-length DUX4 demonstrated that the F67A mutant suppressed 70% of induced genes by more than twofold, or 41% of induced genes by more than fourfold, whereas the iDUX4-CTD showed 90 or 52% suppression, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The F67A mutant suppressed 41% of IFNγ-induced genes by more than fourfold.
source: RNA sequencing analysis using the same criteria to characterize ISG suppression by the full-length DUX4 demonstrated that the F67A mutant suppressed 70% of induced genes by more than twofold, or 41% of induced genes by more than fourfold, whereas the iDUX4-CTD showed 90 or 52% suppression, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The iDUX4-CTD suppressed 90% of IFNγ-induced genes by more than twofold.
source: RNA sequencing analysis using the same criteria to characterize ISG suppression by the full-length DUX4 demonstrated that the F67A mutant suppressed 70% of induced genes by more than twofold, or 41% of induced genes by more than fourfold, whereas the iDUX4-CTD showed 90 or 52% suppression, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The iDUX4-CTD suppressed 52% of IFNγ-induced genes by more than fourfold.
source: RNA sequencing analysis using the same criteria to characterize ISG suppression by the full-length DUX4 demonstrated that the F67A mutant suppressed 70% of induced genes by more than twofold, or 41% of induced genes by more than fourfold, whereas the iDUX4-CTD showed 90 or 52% suppression, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: DUX4 transcriptional activity is not necessary to suppress IFNγ-mediated gene induction.
source: Together, these data indicate that DUX4 transcriptional activity is not necessary to suppress IFNγ-mediated gene induction.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that transcriptionally inactive DUX4 constructs (F67A and CTD) still suppress ISGs.

claim: The DUX4-CTD contains a pair of (L)LxxL(L) motifs, LLDELL and LLEEL, that are conserved across the DUXC/DUX4 family.
source: The DUX4-CTD contains a pair of (L)LxxL(L) motifs, LLDELL and LLEEL, that are conserved across the DUXC/DUX4 family (Leidenroth and Hewitt, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Leidenroth and Hewitt, 2010).

claim: DUX4 transgenes with mutations in the first motif, deletion of the second motif, or both (iDUX4mL1, iDUX4dL2, iDUX4mL1dL2) failed to activate the DUX4 target ZSCAN4.
source: DUX4 transgenes with mutations in the first motif, deletion of the second motif, or both (iDUX4mL1, iDUX4dL2, iDUX4mL1dL2) (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1B for sequences of these mutants) failed to activate the DUX4 target ZSCAN4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: iDUX4ml1dl2 lost the ability to suppress the panel of ISGs.
source: iDUX4ml1dl2 and iDUX4dl2 both lost the ability to suppress the panel of ISGs, whereas iDUX4mL1 showed partial activity, suppressing three of the four ISGs (Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: iDUX4dl2 lost the ability to suppress the panel of ISGs.
source: iDUX4ml1dl2 and iDUX4dl2 both lost the ability to suppress the panel of ISGs, whereas iDUX4mL1 showed partial activity, suppressing three of the four ISGs (Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: iDUX4mL1 showed partial activity, suppressing three of the four ISGs.
source: iDUX4ml1dl2 and iDUX4dl2 both lost the ability to suppress the panel of ISGs, whereas iDUX4mL1 showed partial activity, suppressing three of the four ISGs (Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The (L)LxxL(L) motifs are necessary for both ISG suppression and for transcriptional activation by DUX4.
source: indicating that these (L)LxxL(L) motifs are necessary for both ISG suppression and for transcriptional activation by DUX4.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that mutations in these motifs abolish both ISG suppression and ZSCAN4 activation.

claim: iDUX4-CTDmL1dL2 did not block the panel of ISGs.
source: Similar to iDUX4mL1dL2, iDUX4-CTDmL1dL2 did not block the panel of ISGs (Figure 2C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: iDUX4aa339-424 maintained ISG suppression, though not as strongly on the IFIH1 and ISG20 genes.
source: The second construct, iDUX4aa339-424, contains only the C-terminal 85 aa residues including both (L)LxxL(L) motifs, and maintained ISG suppression, though not as strongly on the IFIH1 and ISG20 genes (Figure 2C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The DUX4-CTD is both necessary and sufficient to suppress a major portion of the ISG response to IFNγ.
source: In summary, these data support a model in which the DUX4-CTD is both necessary and sufficient to suppress a major portion of the ISG response to IFNγ.

claim: DDX3X is a candidate DUX4-CTD interactor identified by mass spectrometry.
source: STAT1 and DDX3X, two key regulators of innate immune signaling, ranked at the top of the list of candidate DUX4-CTD interactors, together with several other proteins implicated in modulating innate immune signaling (Figure 3, left panel, and Supplementary file 2).

claim: Western blot analysis validated the DUX4-CTD interactions with DDX3X, STAT1, PRKDC, YBX1, HNRNPM, PABPC1, NCL, CDK4, and HNRPU.

evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The region of DUX4 between amino acids 271 and 372 was necessary for co-IP of STAT1.
source: The region of DUX4 between amino acids 271 and 372 was necessary for co-IP of STAT1, whereas the region between 372 and 424 containing the (L)LxxL(L) motifs might enhance DUX4-CTD binding to the phosphorylated forms of STAT1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments with truncation mutants shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The region between 372 and 424 containing the (L)LxxL(L) motifs might enhance DUX4-CTD binding to the phosphorylated forms of STAT1.
source: The region of DUX4 between amino acids 271 and 372 was necessary for co-IP of STAT1, whereas the region between 372 and 424 containing the (L)LxxL(L) motifs might enhance DUX4-CTD binding to the phosphorylated forms of STAT1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DUX4-CTD interacts with STAT1 phospho-Y701 in the absence of phospho-S727.
source: Our studies show that DUX4-CTD interacts with STAT1 phospho-Y701 in the absence of phospho-S727 (i.e., binds the S727A STAT1 mutant), yet also efficiently co-immunoprecipitates with STAT1 phospho-S727 from cell lysates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments with STAT1 mutants shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DUX4-CTD efficiently co-immunoprecipitates with STAT1 phospho-S727 from cell lysates.
source: Our studies show that DUX4-CTD interacts with STAT1 phospho-Y701 in the absence of phospho-S727 (i.e., binds the S727A STAT1 mutant), yet also efficiently co-immunoprecipitates with STAT1 phospho-S727 from cell lysates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Wild-type STAT1 and STAT1-S727A showed enhanced binding to the CTD with IFNγ treatment while the STAT1-Y701A did not.
source: The αMYC signal of the IFNγ-treated samples suggests that our iSTAT1, iSTAT1-Y701A, and iSTAT1-S727A transgenes are expressed at similar levels, and yet the wild-type STAT1 and STAT1-S727A showed enhanced binding to the CTD with IFNγ treatment while the STAT1-Y701A did not (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DUX4-CTD expression did not alter the localization of STAT1 in either untreated cells or IFNγ-treated cells.
source: Furthermore, immunofluorescence showed that DUX4-CTD expression, which was highly restricted to the nucleus, did not alter the localization of STAT1 in either untreated cells (low levels throughout the cell) or IFNγ-treated cells (high levels in the nucleus) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: There was no detectable pSTAT1-Y701 present in the nuclei of untreated cells.
source: Similarly, there was no detectable pSTAT1-Y701 present in the nuclei of untreated cells, but there was a strong pSTAT1-Y701 signal in IFNγ-treated nuclei (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was a strong pSTAT1-Y701 signal in IFNγ-treated nuclei.
source: Similarly, there was no detectable pSTAT1-Y701 present in the nuclei of untreated cells, but there was a strong pSTAT1-Y701 signal in IFNγ-treated nuclei (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The distribution of total STAT1 in the immortalized MB135iDUX4-CTD cells was similar to that in primary human fibroblasts and both immortalized and primary MB135 myoblasts.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of total STAT1 in the immortalized MB135iDUX4-CTD cells was similar to that in primary human fibroblasts and both immortalized and primary MB135 myoblasts, indicating that the immortalization did not alter the distribution of total STAT1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Proximity ligation assay (PLA) indicated close interaction between the iDUX4-CTD and endogenous pSTAT1-Y701 in the nuclei of MB135 cells treated with doxycycline and IFNγ.
source: Proximity ligation assay (PLA) indicated close interaction between the iDUX4-CTD and endogenous pSTAT1-Y701 in the nuclei of MB135 cells treated with doxycycline and IFNγ (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by PLA data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PLA showed an interaction of total STAT1 and DUX4-CTD in primary human fibroblasts.
source: and PLA similarly showed an interaction of total STAT1 and DUX4-CTD in primary human fibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PLA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The interaction between DUX4-CTD and STAT1 is enhanced by phosphorylation of STAT1-Y701.
source: Therefore, the interaction between DUX4-CTD and STAT1 is enhanced by phosphorylation of STAT1-Y701, and we can observe this interaction within the nuclei of DUX4-CTD-expressing cells.
evidence: This is inferred from co-IP and PLA experiments showing enhanced interaction with phosphorylated STAT1.

claim: Treatment with IFNγ following induction of DUX4-CTD diminished STAT1 occupancy at GBP1, IDO1, and CXCL10 promoters.
source: Compared to a gene-desert region where there should not be STAT1 binding (h16q21), there was a robust induction of STAT1 binding following IFNγ treatment at the promoters of several ISGs (GBP1, IDO1, CXCL10) with previously characterized STAT1 binding sites (Rosowski et al., 2014; Figure 5A, left four panels). Treatment with IFNγ following induction of DUX4-CTD diminished STAT1 occupancy at all three ISGs
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The DUX4-CTD robustly suppressed the RNA induction of GBP1, IDO1, and CXCL10 by IFNγ.
source: and paired RT-qPCR confirmed that the DUX4-CTD robustly suppressed the RNA induction by IFNγ (Figure 5A, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: DUX4-CTD blocked Pol-II recruitment to ISGs without affecting occupancy at other genes.
source: We used CUT&Tag (Cleavage Under Target & Tagmentation) (Kaya-Okur et al., 2019) to assess Pol-II occupancy genome wide and found that DUX4-CTD blocked Pol-II recruitment to ISGs without affecting occupancy at other genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The majority of EWSR1 fusion-negative small blue round cell sarcomas have a genetic re-arrangement between CIC and DUX4 that creates a fusion protein containing the carboxyterminal (L)LxxL(L) motif region of DUX4.
source: The majority of EWSR1 fusion-negative small blue round cell sarcomas have a genetic re-arrangement between CIC and DUX4 that creates a fusion protein containing the carboxyterminal (L)LxxL(L) motif region of DUX4 (Graham et al., 2012; Kawamura-Saito et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The Kitra-SRS sarcoma cell line expresses a CIC-DUX4 fusion mRNA containing the terminal 98 amino acids of DUX4.
source: We confirmed that the Kitra-SRS sarcoma cell line expresses a CIC-DUX4 fusion mRNA containing the terminal 98 amino acids of DUX4 as previously described (Nakai et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Nakai et al., 2019).

claim: Kitra-SRS cells showed absent-to-low induction of ISGs when treated with IFNγ and control siRNAs.
source: Compared to MB135 myoblasts, Kitra-SRS cells showed absent-to-low induction of ISGs when treated with IFNγ and control siRNAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: siRNA knockdown of the CIC-DUX4 fusion in the KitraSRS cells resulted in a substantially increased IFNγ induction of ISGs.
source: In contrast, siRNA knockdown of the CIC-DUX4 fusion in the KitraSRS cells resulted in a substantially increased IFNγ induction of ISGs, whereas knockdown of CIC in the MB135 cells did not alter ISG induction (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdown of CIC in the MB135 cells did not alter ISG induction.
source: In contrast, siRNA knockdown of the CIC-DUX4 fusion in the KitraSRS cells resulted in a substantially increased IFNγ induction of ISGs, whereas knockdown of CIC in the MB135 cells did not alter ISG induction (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The CIC-DUX4 fusion suppressed IFNγ induction of ISGs IFIH1, CXCL9, and CD74, although not ISG20.
source: To confirm that the CIC-DUX4 fusion was suppressing ISG induction, we expressed a doxycycline-inducible CIC or the Kitra-SRS CIC-DUX4 fusion protein in MB135 cells and showed that the CIC-DUX4 fusion, but not CIC, suppressed IFNγ induction of ISGs IFIH1, CXCL9, and CD74, although not ISG20 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: CIC did not suppress IFNγ induction of ISGs IFIH1, CXCL9, and CD74.
source: To confirm that the CIC-DUX4 fusion was suppressing ISG induction, we expressed a doxycycline-inducible CIC or the Kitra-SRS CIC-DUX4 fusion protein in MB135 cells and showed that the CIC-DUX4 fusion, but not CIC, suppressed IFNγ induction of ISGs IFIH1, CXCL9, and CD74, although not ISG20 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PLAs were consistent with an interaction of both total STAT1 and phosphorylated STAT1-Y701 with the CIC-DUX4 fusion in the nuclei of Kitra-SRS cells.
source: Furthermore, PLAs were consistent with an interaction of both total STAT1 and phosphorylated STAT1-Y701 with the CIC-DUX4 fusion in the nuclei of Kitra-SRS cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PLA data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Knockdown of the endogenous CIC in MB135 myoblasts had no effect on MHC I response to IFNγ.
source: We found that knockdown of the endogenous CIC in MB135 myoblasts had no effect on MHC I response to IFNγ (54.9% in siCTRL+ IFNγ compared to 60.7% in siCIC-DUX4+ IFNγ, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of the CIC-DUX4 fusion protein in Kitra-SRS cells almost doubled the number of MHC I-positive cells with IFNγ treatment.
source: In contrast, knockdown of the CIC-DUX4 fusion protein in Kitra-SRS cells almost doubled the number of MHC I-positive cells with IFNγ treatment (48.1%) compared to cells treated with siCTRL and IFNγ (27.9%, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In cultured FSHD myotubes, approximately 5% of the myotubes might express DUX4 in their nuclei.
source: In cultured FSHD myotubes, approximately 5% of the myotubes might express DUX4 in their nuclei.
evidence: This is a statement about DUX4 expression patterns in FSHD myotubes, supported by prior work in the field.

claim: Treatment with IFNγ produced a reliable IDO1 signal within the nucleus and cytoplasm of individual myotubes that did not express DUX4.
source: Treatment with IFNγ produced a reliable IDO1 signal within the nucleus and cytoplasm of individual myotubes that did not express DUX4, whereas DUX4-positive myotubes did not show IDO1 expression in response to IFNγ
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: DUX4-positive myotubes did not show IDO1 expression in response to IFNγ.
source: Treatment with IFNγ produced a reliable IDO1 signal within the nucleus and cytoplasm of individual myotubes that did not express DUX4, whereas DUX4-positive myotubes did not show IDO1 expression in response to IFNγ
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Endogenous DUX4 expressed at a physiological level is sufficient to prevent ISG induction by IFNγ.
source: Therefore, similar to our MB135-iDUX4 studies, endogenous DUX4 expressed at a physiological level is sufficient to prevent ISG induction by IFNγ.
evidence: This is inferred from immunofluorescence experiments in FSHD myotubes shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Dux, the mouse ortholog of human DUX4, is expressed at the equivalent developmental stage to human DUX4.
source: Dux, the mouse ortholog of human DUX4, is expressed at the equivalent developmental stage to human DUX4 (Hendrickson et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Hendrickson et al., 2017).

claim: Mouse Dux activates a parallel transcriptional program to human DUX4.
source: activates a parallel transcriptional program (Whiddon et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Whiddon et al., 2017).

claim: Mouse Dux contains the (L)LxxL(L) motifs.
source: and contains the (L)LxxL(L) motifs that we have shown to be necessary for ISG repression by human DUX4.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mouse Dux sequence contains a 60 amino acid triplication of the (L)LxxL(L)-containing region.
source: In fact, the mouse Dux sequence contains a 60 amino acid triplication of the (L)LxxL(L)-containing region (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The full-length Dux protein repressed the panel of ISGs even more robustly than the full-length or CTD portion of human DUX4.
source: Accordingly, we introduced a doxycycline-inducible mouse Dux transgene into human MB135 cells (MB135-iDux) and found that the full-length Dux protein repressed the panel of ISGs even more robustly than the full-length or CTD portion of human DUX4 (Figure 7B, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Western analysis confirmed the co-immunoprecipitation of STAT1 and both phosphorylated pSTAT1-Y701 and pSTAT1-S727 with mouse Dux.
source: Similar to human DUX4, Western analysis confirmed the co-immunoprecipitation of STAT1 and both phosphorylated pSTAT1-Y701 and pSTAT1-S727 with mouse Dux (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The suppression of ISG induction and interaction with phosphorylated STAT1 is conserved in the DUXC family.
source: These data demonstrate that the suppression of ISG induction and interaction with phosphorylated STAT1 is conserved in the DUXC family.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that both human DUX4 and mouse Dux suppress ISGs and interact with STAT1.

claim: The DUX4-CTD colocalizes with STAT1 in the nucleus.
source: In this study, we show that the DUX4-CTD, a transcriptionally inactive carboxyterminal fragment of DUX4, is necessary and sufficient to broadly suppress ISG induction by IFNγ as well as partially inhibit induction through the IFNβ, cGAS, IFIH1/MDA5, and DDX58/RIG-I pathways. The DUX4-CTD colocalizes with STAT1 in the nucleus, diminishes steady-state STAT1 occupancy at ISG promoters, and prevents Pol-II recruitment and transcriptional activation of ISGs by IFNγ.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PLA experiments shown in Figures 4C and 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The DUX4-CTD diminishes steady-state STAT1 occupancy at ISG promoters.
source: The DUX4-CTD colocalizes with STAT1 in the nucleus, diminishes steady-state STAT1 occupancy at ISG promoters, and prevents Pol-II recruitment and transcriptional activation of ISGs by IFNγ.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The DUX4-CTD prevents Pol-II recruitment and transcriptional activation of ISGs by IFNγ.
source: The DUX4-CTD colocalizes with STAT1 in the nucleus, diminishes steady-state STAT1 occupancy at ISG promoters, and prevents Pol-II recruitment and transcriptional activation of ISGs by IFNγ.
evidence: This is demonstrated by CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The conserved DUX4 (L)LxxL(L) motifs are necessary to suppress transcriptional activation by STAT1.
source: Whereas the conserved DUX4 (L)LxxL(L) motifs are necessary to suppress transcriptional activation by STAT1, they are not necessary for the interaction of DUX4 and STAT1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with mutant constructs shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The conserved DUX4 (L)LxxL(L) motifs are not necessary for the interaction of DUX4 and STAT1.
source: Whereas the conserved DUX4 (L)LxxL(L) motifs are necessary to suppress transcriptional activation by STAT1, they are not necessary for the interaction of DUX4 and STAT1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IFNγ binding to its receptor, IFNGR, leads to the phosphorylation of STAT1 at Y701.
source: IFNγ binding to its receptor, IFNGR, leads to the phosphorylation of STAT1 at Y701, subsequently STAT1 forms a homodimer, translocates to the nucleus, and binds the gamma-activated sequence (GAS) in the promoters of ISGs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the IFNγ signaling pathway.

claim: STAT1 forms a homodimer after phosphorylation at Y701.
source: IFNγ binding to its receptor, IFNGR, leads to the phosphorylation of STAT1 at Y701, subsequently STAT1 forms a homodimer, translocates to the nucleus, and binds the gamma-activated sequence (GAS) in the promoters of ISGs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the IFNγ signaling pathway.

claim: STAT1 translocates to the nucleus after forming a homodimer.
source: IFNγ binding to its receptor, IFNGR, leads to the phosphorylation of STAT1 at Y701, subsequently STAT1 forms a homodimer, translocates to the nucleus, and binds the gamma-activated sequence (GAS) in the promoters of ISGs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the IFNγ signaling pathway.

claim: STAT1 binds the gamma-activated sequence (GAS) in the promoters of ISGs.
source: IFNγ binding to its receptor, IFNGR, leads to the phosphorylation of STAT1 at Y701, subsequently STAT1 forms a homodimer, translocates to the nucleus, and binds the gamma-activated sequence (GAS) in the promoters of ISGs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the IFNγ signaling pathway.

claim: DNA-bound STAT1 is additionally phosphorylated at S727 and recruits Pol-II to the ISG promoters.
source: DNA-bound STAT1 is additionally phosphorylated at S727 and recruits Pol-II to the ISG promoters (Sadzak et al., 2008; Wen et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: DUX4-CTD interacts with STAT1 phospho-Y701 but DNA binding of this complex is not fully impaired because of the association with STAT1 phospho-727.
source: Our studies show that DUX4-CTD interacts with STAT1 phospho-Y701 in the absence of phospho-S727 (i.e., binds the S727A STAT1 mutant), yet also efficiently co-immunoprecipitates with STAT1 phospho-S727 from cell lysates. This indicates that despite DUX4 interacting with STAT1 phospho-Y701, DNA binding of this complex is not fully impaired because of the association with STAT1 phospho-727.
evidence: This is inferred from co-IP experiments showing that DUX4 binds both Y701-phosphorylated and S727-phosphorylated STAT1.

claim: ChIP and CUT&Tag studies show decreased STAT1 steady-state occupancy of ISG promoters and failure to recruit Pol-II in the presence of DUX4-CTD.
source: However, our ChIP and CUT&Tag studies show decreased STAT1 steady-state occupancy of ISG promoters and failure to recruit Pol-II.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP data in Figure 5A and CUT&Tag data in Figure 5B.

claim: DUX4 interaction with pSTAT1-Y701 prevents the formation of a stable DNA-bound complex and recruitment of Pol-II.
source: Together, these data support a model of DUX4 interaction with pSTAT1-Y701 that prevents the formation of a stable DNA-bound complex and recruitment of Pol-II, but likely not the initial binding of STAT1 to DNA because of the abundance of phospho-S727 associated with DUX4.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The (L)LxxL(L) motifs are necessary to prevent transcriptional activation, presumably by blocking Pol-II recruitment.
source: The (L)LxxL(L) motifs are necessary to prevent transcriptional activation, presumably by blocking Pol-II recruitment, but not necessary for the interaction of DUX4 with STAT1.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that mutations in these motifs abolish ISG suppression but not STAT1 interaction.

claim: Blocking Pol-II recruitment by DUX4 could be due to recruitment of a repressor or by simply blocking the interaction of STAT1 with an intermediate factor necessary to recruit Pol-II.
source: This could be due to recruitment of a repressor or by simply blocking the interaction of STAT1 with an intermediate factor necessary to recruit Pol-II.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: The (L)LxxL(L)-dependent inhibition of STAT1 by DUX4 bears a striking similarity to the inhibitory mechanisms displayed by LxxLL-containing members of the PIAS family.
source: The (L)LxxL(L)-dependent inhibition of STAT1 by DUX4 in this study bears a striking similarity to the inhibitory mechanisms displayed by LxxLL-containing members of the PIAS family.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of DUX4 mechanisms with known PIAS mechanisms.

claim: LxxLL motifs facilitate protein-protein interactions between unbound NRs and co-repressors such as RIP140 and HDACs.
source: LxxLL motifs were first identified in nuclear-receptor (NR) signaling pathways (Heery et al., 1997) where they were found to facilitate protein-protein interactions between unbound NRs and co-repressors such as RIP140 and HDACs, or agonist-bound NRs and co-activators such as CBP/p300 (Plevin et al., 2005; Savkur and Burris, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: LxxLL motifs facilitate protein-protein interactions between agonist-bound NRs and co-activators such as CBP/p300.
source: LxxLL motifs were first identified in nuclear-receptor (NR) signaling pathways (Heery et al., 1997) where they were found to facilitate protein-protein interactions between unbound NRs and co-repressors such as RIP140 and HDACs, or agonist-bound NRs and co-activators such as CBP/p300 (Plevin et al., 2005; Savkur and Burris, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: LxxLL motifs have been characterized in multiple protein families, including the PIAS family, and specifically implicated in modulating immune transcriptional networks via interaction with and inhibition of STATs, IRFs, and NF-kB.
source: LxxLL motifs have since been characterized in multiple protein families, including the PIAS family, and specifically implicated in modulating immune transcriptional networks via interaction with and inhibition of STATs, IRFs, and NF-kB (Shuai and Liu, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Shuai and Liu, 2005).

claim: The (L)LxxL(L) region of DUX4 is required for suppression of IFNγ-mediated ISG induction and its enhanced interaction with pSTAT1-Y701.
source: While the (L)LxxL(L) region of DUX4 is required for suppression of IFNγ-mediated ISG induction and its enhanced interaction with pSTAT1-Y701, it is not required for its apparently weaker interaction with unphosphorylated STAT1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with mutant constructs shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The (L)LxxL(L) region of DUX4 is not required for its apparently weaker interaction with unphosphorylated STAT1.
source: While the (L)LxxL(L) region of DUX4 is required for suppression of IFNγ-mediated ISG induction and its enhanced interaction with pSTAT1-Y701, it is not required for its apparently weaker interaction with unphosphorylated STAT1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The LxxLL motif of PIASγ is not required for initial binding to STAT1, but is required to suppress ISG induction mediated by STAT1 in response to both IFNβ and IFNγ.
source: In a similar manner, the LxxLL motif of PIASγ is not required for initial binding to STAT1, but is required to suppress ISG induction mediated by STAT1 in response to both IFNβ (Kubota et al., 2011) and IFNγ (Liu et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The LxxLL motif is required for the trans-repression of androgen receptor (AR) signaling by PIASγ.
source: The same motif is required for the trans-repression of androgen receptor (AR) signaling by PIASγ (Gross et al., 2001) and of Erythroid Krüppel-like factor (EKLF or KLF1) by PIAS3 (Siatecka et al., 2015), though again it is not required for the initial interaction of either pair.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Gross et al., 2001).

claim: The LxxLL motif is required for the trans-repression of Erythroid Krüppel-like factor (EKLF or KLF1) by PIAS3.
source: The same motif is required for the trans-repression of androgen receptor (AR) signaling by PIASγ (Gross et al., 2001) and of Erythroid Krüppel-like factor (EKLF or KLF1) by PIAS3 (Siatecka et al., 2015), though again it is not required for the initial interaction of either pair.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Siatecka et al., 2015).

claim: PIAS proteins can suppress transcriptional networks by blocking DNA binding, as with PIAS3 and STAT3.
source: Additionally, just as DUX4 reduces the steady-state occupancy of STAT1 to DNA, PIAS proteins can suppress transcriptional networks by blocking DNA binding, as with PIAS3 and STAT3 (Chung et al., 1997) or PIAS1 and NF-kB p65 (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Chung et al., 1997).

claim: PIAS proteins can suppress transcriptional networks by blocking DNA binding, as with PIAS1 and NF-kB p65.
source: Additionally, just as DUX4 reduces the steady-state occupancy of STAT1 to DNA, PIAS proteins can suppress transcriptional networks by blocking DNA binding, as with PIAS3 and STAT3 (Chung et al., 1997) or PIAS1 and NF-kB p65 (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Liu et al., 2005).

claim: The DUXC family likely evolved target specificity through the larger areas of conservation around the (L)LxxL(L) motifs.
source: It is important to emphasize that the xx amino acids in the DUXC family are acidic and there is conservation of flanking amino acids as well, suggesting that the DUXC family likely evolved target specificity through these larger areas of conservation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on sequence analysis.

claim: DDX3X has been shown to regulate RNA processing, translation, and innate immune signaling.
source: DDX3X has been shown to regulate RNA processing, translation, and innate immune signaling (Mo et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Mo et al., 2021).

claim: DDX3X acts as a scaffolding factor necessary for IKK-ε and TBK1 phosphorylation of IRFs.
source: It was also shown to be a pathway-specific regulator of IRF3 and IRF7 in part by acting as a scaffolding factor necessary for IKK-ε and TBK1 phosphorylation of IRFs (Gu et al., 2013; Schröder et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: DDX3X is a sensor of dsRNA and viral stem-loop RNA with a role in the initial induction of ISGs, including IFIH1 and DDX58.
source: DDX3X was also shown to be a sensor of dsRNA and viral stem-loop RNA with a role in the initial induction of ISGs, including IFIH1 and DDX58 (Oshiumi et al., 2010) that then serve to amplify the signaling mechanisms.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Oshiumi et al., 2010).

claim: PRKDC is known mostly for its major roles in DNA repair but also has been implicated in regulating the response to cytoplasmic DNA through the cGAS and IRF3 pathway.
source: PRKDC is known mostly for its major roles in DNA repair but also has been implicated in regulating the response to cytoplasmic DNA through the cGAS and IRF3 pathway (Ferguson et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Ferguson et al., 2012).

claim: The full-length DUX4 is expressed in a diverse set of solid cancers.
source: Previously we reported that the full-length DUX4 is expressed in a diverse set of solid cancers (Chew et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior published work (Chew et al., 2019).

claim: Cancers expressing DUX4 had diminished IFNγ-induced MHC class I expression.
source: Cancers expressing DUX4 had diminished IFNγ-induced MHC class I expression, reduced anti-tumor immune cell infiltration, and showed resistance to immune checkpoint blockade.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior published work (Chew et al., 2019) as cited in the introduction.

claim: Cancers expressing DUX4 had reduced anti-tumor immune cell infiltration.
source: Cancers expressing DUX4 had diminished IFNγ-induced MHC class I expression, reduced anti-tumor immune cell infiltration, and showed resistance to immune checkpoint blockade.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior published work (Chew et al., 2019) as cited in the introduction.

claim: Cancers expressing DUX4 showed resistance to immune checkpoint blockade.
source: Cancers expressing DUX4 had diminished IFNγ-induced MHC class I expression, reduced anti-tumor immune cell infiltration, and showed resistance to immune checkpoint blockade.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior published work (Chew et al., 2019) as cited in the introduction.

claim: The CIC-DUX4 fusion protein contains the terminal 98 amino acids of DUX4, aa327-424, that encompasses a region shown to be sufficient to suppress IFNγ signaling.
source: In this study, we show that the CIC-DUX4 fusion in EWSR1-fusion-negative sarcomas blocks IFNγ-induced ISG expression and the upregulation of MHC I. This fusion protein contains the terminal 98 amino acids of DUX4, aa327-424, that encompasses a region shown to be sufficient to suppress IFNγ signaling in the iDUX4-aa339-424 (see Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The fusion protein in the CIC-DUX4 sarcomas, or the full-length DUX4 in some other cancers, contributes to immune evasion at least in part through its interaction with STAT1.
source: It is reasonable to suggest that this fusion protein in the CIC-DUX4 sarcomas, or the full-length DUX4 in some other cancers, contributes to immune evasion at least in part through its interaction with STAT1, and that targeting DUX4 or its interaction with STAT1 might improve immune-based therapies for DUX4-expressing cancers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Targeting DUX4 or its interaction with STAT1 might improve immune-based therapies for DUX4-expressing cancers.
source: It is reasonable to suggest that this fusion protein in the CIC-DUX4 sarcomas, or the full-length DUX4 in some other cancers, contributes to immune evasion at least in part through its interaction with STAT1, and that targeting DUX4 or its interaction with STAT1 might improve immune-based therapies for DUX4-expressing cancers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic implications.

claim: The conservation of the (L)LxxL(L) motifs in mouse Dux and its similar interaction with STAT1 and inhibition of IFNγ signaling indicates that this is a conserved function of the DUXC family.
source: The conservation of the (L)LxxL(L) motifs in mouse Dux and its similar interaction with STAT1 and inhibition of IFNγ signaling indicates that this is a conserved function of the DUXC family.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that both human DUX4 and mouse Dux have similar mechanisms.

claim: DUX4, Dux, and the canine DUXC all induce expression of endogenous retroelements.
source: DUX4, Dux, and the canine DUXC all induce expression of endogenous retroelements, as well as pericentromeric satellite repeats that form dsRNAs that, at least in the case of DUX4, induce a dsRNA response that results in activation of PKR and phosphorylation of EIF2α (Shadle et al., 2019; Shadle et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: DUX4, Dux, and the canine DUXC all induce expression of pericentromeric satellite repeats that form dsRNAs.
source: DUX4, Dux, and the canine DUXC all induce expression of endogenous retroelements, as well as pericentromeric satellite repeats that form dsRNAs that, at least in the case of DUX4, induce a dsRNA response that results in activation of PKR and phosphorylation of EIF2α (Shadle et al., 2019; Shadle et al., 2017).

claim: In the case of DUX4, pericentromeric satellite repeats induce a dsRNA response that results in activation of PKR and phosphorylation of EIF2α.
